stories.headline: Brazil’s Lula and Flávio Bolsonaro clash in first presidential runoff debate

sources.body: Brazilian President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva and right-wing senator Flavio Bolsonaro traded personal attacks in a heated presidential debate on Sunday, a week before a closely contested runoff. The rivals accused each other of lying and corruption while clashing over the economy, security and healthcare ahead of the October 25 vote.
sources.headline: Brazil's Lula, Bolsonaro clash in bitter debate ahead of election runoff

sources.body:
Brazil’s president and his opponent lob a barrage of attacks on each other in debate a week before the October 25 vote.

Brazil’s President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva and right-wing Senator Flavio Bolsonaro fired off a barrage of personal attacks during their first debate a week before a tight presidential run-off.

In a chaotic exchange on Sunday, the two men called each other “liar” multiple times, accused each other of corruption, dragged up various scandals, and clashed on issues from public security to healthcare.

Lula said Bolsonaro was “a habitual liar” and a “thug”, and physically distanced himself on stage from the candidate he called a “militiaman”, alluding to his alleged ties to Rio de Janeiro’s paramilitary groups.

Bolsonaro, who led the first-round election with 47 percent to Lula’s 45 percent, said it was better to keep Lula at a distance “because my wallet could be stolen”.

Throughout the debate, Bolsonaro, 45, the son of former President Jair Bolsonaro, paced behind Lula, shaking his head, smirking and scoffing as his adversary spoke.

The 80-year-old Lula, who is seeking a fourth term, demanded an explanation regarding a corruption investigation involving the older Bolsonaro, a question his opponent dodged.

The younger Bolsonaro responded by calling Lula a “clown”, and then parried by bringing up a potential corruption case involving one of the president’s sons.

Jair Bolsonaro has been under house arrest while serving a 27-year sentence connected to efforts to overturn the 2022 election, which he lost to Lula.

Flavio Bolsonaro hammered away at the top concerns of Brazilians, such as the cost of living and crime, and accused Lula of “reckless spending” to get re-elected, referring to various social measures the president has announced during the campaign.

Lula countered by asking Bolsonaro about his plans to emulate the drastic public spending cuts implemented by Argentina’s right-wing president, Javier Milei.

Bolsonaro dodged the question throughout the debate and pivoted to different topics.

When his father’s handling of the COVID-19 pandemic came up, Bolsonaro admitted that this “wasn’t an area where we saw the best results during Bolsonaro’s presidency. I’ll offer a mea culpa here.”

Lula also sought to portray his opponent as out of touch with poor Brazilians, saying Bolsonaro had never used the country’s public healthcare system or taken a bus.

“My opponent only knows about buses from books. He has never even stepped foot on one. He has no idea what the world of work is like,” Lula said.

Ahead of Sunday’s debate, supporters of each candidate gathered en masse in public to show their allegiance.

Pro-Bolsonaro crowds wearing Brazil’s national colours of yellow, green and blue packed Paulista Avenue in Sao Paulo’s financial centre, where the candidate addressed the crowd.

Lula supporters wearing red, symbolic of his Workers’ Party, filled Brasilia’s plaza of government buildings, while students backing the president protested against Bolsonaro in Rio de Janeiro.
sources.headline: Lula and Bolsonaro spar in Brazil’s fiery first presidential run-off debate

stories.headline: Ukraine’s large drone attack hits Saint Petersburg oil facilities

sources.body: A large-scale Ukrainian drone attack on Russia's second-largest city Saint Petersburg killed at least one person and hospitalised another five on Sunday. The attack – which also sparked fires at an oil refinery and depot – comes as Kyiv accused Russia of violating Washington's "energy ceasefire" dozens of times.
sources.headline: Ukrainian drone attack on Saint Petersburg kills one, sets refinery ablaze

sources.body:
At least one person has been killed in an overnight attack on St Petersburg that successfully targeted two of the city's oil facilities.

The region's Governor Alexander Beglov said fires were being extinguished at the St Petersburg Oil Terminal and the Ruchyi oil depot following the attack, which also injured at least five.

A logistics centre belonging to Ozon - known as Russia's Amazon - and a data centre belonging to Facebook equivalent VKontakte were also hit.

Kyiv has not yet commented on the strikes. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky said on Saturday morning that Russia had targeted his country's energy sector 76 times since Donald Trump declared an "energy ceasefire" last week.

Ukraine had paused its strikes on Russian oil facilities - which it says are to limit the main revenue stream for Moscow's war effort - for three days after the announcement, while accusing Russia of continuing.

It then resumed strikes earlier this week, drawing the ire of Trump, who called for a truce to facilitate a deal he struck with his Russian counterpart Vladimir Putin to supply diesel.

Ukraine has struck St Petersburg before, though regions closer to Ukraine are threatened more often. The city's oil terminal was last hit in July .

Russia's defence ministry said it had shot down more than 1,000 Ukrainian drones over Russian territory overnight into Sunday.

St Petersburg's governor said 12 apartment buildings and two homes were damaged in the attacks on the city, while Pulkovo Airport was temporarily closed.

He also said mobile internet service disruption was possible.

Social network VK confirmed a drone had targeted its regional data centre, but stressed its services were available "as usual" after users reported outages in the early hours of the morning.

Ozon also confirmed its local logistics centre had been targeted by a drone, sparking a fire.

It said staff were evacuated and no one was injured, and that it was not accepting shipments from sellers at the location "as it is currently serving other operational purposes".

As well as numerous oil facilities across Russia, Ukraine has also mounted strikes aimed at disrupting the Russian economy more broadly. Earlier this month, it launched a series of attacks on Yandex, Russia's largest search engine, that led to service disruptions.

Relations between Washington and Kyiv have frayed since the US struck a controversial deal to import Russian diesel in the hope of bringing down US energy prices, which have skyrocketed during the Iran war, ahead of the midterm elections.

Zelensky suggested the deal was tantamount to the US investing in Russia's war effort.

Trump's decision to temporarily suspend a raft of sanctions against Russia has brought fresh criticism , including from some US Republicans.

However, on Sunday, Zelensky said on Telegram he had had conversations with Trump's top negotiators Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner.

He said their teams are in constant communication and preparing the next diplomatic steps.

Both Russia and Ukraine have been striking one another's energy infrastructure with increasing intensity ahead of the winter, as Moscow's full-scale invasion drags on in its fifth year.
sources.headline: Oil facilities hit in deadly overnight attack on St Petersburg

stories.headline: Trump defends easing Russia sanctions as Ukraine peace talks strain

sources.body:
US President Donald Trump has said his decision to suspend several Russian sanctions is an effort to keep Moscow at the negotiating table.

"I am in the process of negotiating Peace in the war between Russia and Ukraine," Trump said on his Truth Social messaging platform, adding that he didn't want to "do anything that will drive, foolishly, Russia away from the bargaining table".

Trump blocked numerous sanctions on Russia on Friday night, two days before they were due to take effect, as a row with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky deepened.

Zelensky told NBC News on Sunday that siding with Russian President Vladimir Putin would be a "historic mistake".

Russian envoy Kirill Dmitriev has responded to Trump's order by calling it "an important and truly historic moment". He said the sanctions, which were passed by the US Congress and signed into law by the US president in September, would have inflicted "serious damage" on the US and global market.

US Secretary of State Marco Rubio has described the suspension of the sanctions as a 60-day pause during which their potential impact on the US and global economies would be analysed.

In his Truth Social post, Trump also said Zelensky "doesn't want to end this war, and probably never did", adding "he could have made a better deal two years ago than he can now".

Zelensky has pushed for an end to fighting, and has repeatedly said that Putin doesn't want peace, since Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022.

Relations between Washington and Kyiv frayed after the US struck a controversial deal to import Russian diesel last week.

Despite the international sanctions, Russia has still been able to export oil, much of it to China and India - often at attractive discounts. According to the think-tank Centre for Research on Energy and Clean Air (CREA), China has taken about half of Russia's crude exports, with India accounting for about 37%.

In remarks to a European Union summit, after Trump announced the deal to buy diesel from Russia and said Zelensky was "more difficult to deal with" than Putin, Zelensky said it was nice to be among "real leaders".

Zelensky has repeatedly pushed for stringent sanctions to limit funding that Russia can use in its war effort. After the latest move from the US, however, he said he believed the Trump administration would lift more sanctions against Russia.

Ukraine and its European allies criticised Trump's plans to import Russian diesel to help lower US energy prices, which have skyrocketed during the Iran war.

The deal, according to Zelensky, was tantamount to the US investing in Russia's war effort.

Concerns that Trump is siding with Russia have been heightened by disruption to Starlink, a US-provided satellite system used by Ukraine. That hampered Kyiv's ability to protect itself from Russian attacks.

Zelensky said US officials had linked speed restrictions to technical issues.

However, he said Ukraine had tested Starlink on EU territory and found it was operating at higher speeds.
sources.headline: Trump says suspension of Russia sanctions is to keep peace negotiations going

sources.body:
US president accuses Ukrainian leader of not wanting to end the war, as Zelenskyy speaks with Washington envoys.

United States President Donald Trump has defended sanction waivers for Russia, saying he wants to keep Moscow at the bargaining table and accusing his counterpart in Kyiv of not wanting to end the war in Ukraine.

Trump made the comments on Truth Social on Sunday in response to criticism of his decision to block numerous sanctions on Russia just days before they were due to take effect.

“My decision on Russia is a very simple one. I am in the process of negotiating Peace in the war between Russia and Ukraine, and don’t want to do anything that will drive, foolishly, Russia away from the bargaining table,” he said.

The move has triggered a significant diplomatic fallout between Trump and Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy over the past week.

Zelenskyy said that waiving sanctions on Russia, which launched a full-scale invasion of its neighbour in 2022, “will hurt Ukraine”, telling NBC’s Meet the Press on Sunday that it would strengthen Russian President Vladimir Putin’s war effort.

“We can’t compare me and Putin. He’s [an] aggressor. He occupied us. He killed adults and children, his soldiers. He’s a terrorist, and that’s why I hope that President Trump will be very clear with this position.”

Trump reiterated his claim that Zelenskyy does not want the war on his country to end, saying on Truth Social that Kyiv was launching attacks on diesel refineries in Russia despite knowing it was “seriously hurting the world diesel markets”.

“Zelenskyy doesn’t care, and frankly, with all of the money that Europe is famously giving him… he doesn’t want to end this war, and probably never did,” Trump wrote.

Trump announced plans on October 9 for Russia to supply more than 300,000 metric tonnes of diesel to US and global markets to tackle fuel prices that have soared since the US and Israel launched war on Iran in late February. The move led Tehran to effectively close the Strait of Hormuz, through which one-fifth of global energy exports transited before the war.

Trump’s embrace of Russian energy has angered not only Kyiv, but also European partners and many US officials, who say the move rewards Moscow while it continues its four-and-a-half-year war against Ukraine.

The Ukrainian president said on X on Sunday that he has spoken with US presidential envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner as part of “virtually non-stop communication” between the two countries’ teams aimed at the “next steps in diplomacy”.

“We are doing everything on our part to make this happen, and to ensure that America’s position is strong and helps bring peace closer. Peace that everyone, except Russia, has been waiting for over the past four and a half years,” Zelenskyy wrote.

Zelenskyy spoke with Witkoff and Kushner as Russia and Ukraine continued to strike each other’s energy sites , with Moscow leaving thousands without power, and Kyiv carrying out the largest drone attack on Russia, in St Petersburg, since the war began.
sources.headline: Trump defends Russian sanctions relief, lashes out at Zelenskyy

sources.body: Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky spoke with US envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner on Sunday amid tensions after President Donald Trump accused Kyiv of resisting peace with Russia. The talks came as both sides exchanged attacks on energy infrastructure, while Washington’s easing of Russian sanctions raised concerns among European allies.
sources.headline: Zelensky holds US talks as Trump accuses him of not wanting peace

stories.headline: Trump endorses Netanyahu ahead of Israel’s election

sources.body:
In a social media post ahead of Israel’s October 27 election, Trump calls Netanyahu a ‘Strong, Brave, and Brilliant’ leader.

United States President Donald Trump has issued an endorsement of Israel’s incumbent Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, who is facing a close race in parliamentary elections scheduled for October 27.

In a post on Truth Social on Sunday, Trump praised the Israeli leader for being an ally of the US in its war on Iran. He added that he was giving his “Complete and Total Endorsement” to Netanyahu.

“BIBI NETANYAHU WILL NEVER LET YOU DOWN!” Trump wrote.

The US president’s backing comes nine days before the Israeli election — and after speculation that it might not come at all.

Trump had refused to endorse Netanyahu earlier this month, when asked repeatedly about the Israeli leader’s job performance in an interview with Time magazine.

Instead, when pressed by his interviewer, Trump avoided the subject, shifting the focus instead to his own popularity or security in the Middle East.

The two leaders have met more than a half dozen times since January 2025, but there have been reports of disagreements, including over the war against Iran and other conflicts.

In June, Trump acknowledged calling Netanyahu “f***ing crazy” in a phone conversation where he expressed frustration about Israel’s attacks on Lebanon.

Trump had reportedly asked Netanyahu not to take further action in Lebanon, in an apparent attempt to preserve a short-lived April ceasefire with Iran.

The two leaders had jointly launched a war against Iran on February 28, but the conflict has cost Trump domestic support.

The war has upended the global oil and gas supply, with no clear end in sight.

A Pew Research Center poll found this month that roughly two-thirds of US voters disapprove of Trump’s handling of the war, which has driven up consumer fuel prices and raised concerns about draining military stockpiles.

Trump’s Republican Party is facing a critical midterm election on November 3 that will decide whether it maintains control of the US Congress, as well as other key state and local offices.

Experts have speculated that Trump’s prior reticence to endorse Netanyahu may have come from public perception that Israel may have coaxed the US into the war.

Netanyahu’s Likud Party and its far-right coalition are also facing the prospect of losing the October contest to an opposition bloc led by Yashar party head Gadi Eisenkot.

But despite reports of fraying relations, Trump told the news outlet Axios on Sunday that his endorsement of Netanyahu was never in doubt.

“I was always going to do that. I just didn’t want to do it too soon,” Trump said in a short telephone interview to the publication, adding: “It is important that Israel has a person they can count on.”

Axios said it questioned Trump about whether he could work with another Israeli leader other than Netanyahu. The US president answered evasively.

“Maybe I will, maybe I won’t. Who wants to take the chance?” Trump replied.

In his social media post announcing the endorsement, Trump also defended his and Netanyahu’s decision to initiate the war against Iran. The president argued it was only a matter of time before Iran would have attacked both the US and Israel.
sources.headline: Trump endorses Netanyahu in Israeli legislative elections

sources.body: US President Donald Trump on Sunday endorsed Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu ahead of Israel's October 27 elections. It was not clear what impact the endorsement would have on voters, since many Israelis have expressed disappointment with Trump over the outcome of the Iran war and the US president's ceasefire proposal.
sources.headline: Trump endorses embattled Israeli PM Netanyahu ahead of October 27 election

stories.headline: Anthropic commits 5% of its shares to a public-benefit fund

sources.body:
Artificial intelligence (AI) giant Anthropic says it will commit 5% of its shares to a fund that will make donations for the "public good".

The announcement comes as Anthropic lays the ground for a potential blockbuster stock market listing that could value the firm at more than $1tn (£750bn).

The AI industry has come under intense scrutiny recently over safety concerns and fears about its impact on society and the economy. Anthropic reportedly said in its initial public offering (IPO) filing that AI could pose "catastrophic or existential risks to humanity".

Anthropic said its proposed fund could support nonprofit organisations, and efforts to address AI's impact on the jobs market.

None of the shares held by the the fund would be used for lobbying or political donations in the US or overseas, it added.

Anthropic's Public Benefit Fund could also receive another 2% of the firm's shares at its board's discretion, the Claude developer said in a statement released on Sunday.

Technology billionaire Elon Musk responded to the announcement on social media with: "I recommend giving the shares directly to the public." "This is what I will be doing," he added.

Last week, Anthropic told prospective investors that its revenue surged by 45% to $16.8bn (£12.6bn) in the three months to the end of September.

In common with other AI firms, it is seeking to position itself as being able to generate huge profits despite spending billions on developing the technology and building infrastructure to power its models.

Companies around the world, primarily technology firms, have cut thousands of jobs after investing in AI, with many pointing to higher efficiencies from its adoption.

Research by the International Monetary Fund (IMF) published in 2024 suggested that almost 40% of jobs around the world will be affected by AI , with that figure rising as high as ​60% in advanced economies.
sources.headline: Anthropic says it will commit 5% of its shares to 'public benefit fund'

sources.body:
Claude creator says fund could used for donations to NGOs and ‘direct distributions to specific populations’.

Anthropic has pledged to commit 5 percent of its shares to a new fund dedicated to the public good, with plans to increase the contribution as the artificial intelligence giant’s market value grows.

The creator of the AI assistant Claude announced the new “Anthropic Public Benefit Fund” on Sunday as tech firms face intense scrutiny over the potential dangers posed by the frontier technology.

In a blog post, Anthropic said it was committing 5 percent of company shares with immediate effect, subject to stockholder approval, with an additional 2 percent to be added “at the board’s discretion” for every 50 percent increase in the company’s value.

“Because of the way the Fund is structured, the more Anthropic grows, the larger the share of the company that can be dedicated expressly to the public good,” the San Francisco-based firm said.

“It is common practice for tech companies to offer escalating compensation awards to their executives. We are instead directing that equity to the public benefit.”

Anthropic said the fund could be used to make donations to traditional nonprofits, as well as “direct distributions to specific populations”.

It said labour market disruption due to AI could be among the causes addressed by the fund.

“Anthropic has already committed $200 million to studying and addressing this issue, but given the pace of AI progress, bolder approaches may be needed,” the company said.

“The Fund will have the versatility to pursue them.”

Anthropic, officially registered as a “public benefit corporation” in the US state of Delaware, said the fund would not be used for lobbying or political donations, either in the United States or overseas.

Founded in 2021 by former employees of ChatGPT creator OpenAI, Anthropic is preparing for what could be the largest public initial offering in history. It is expected to list on the US stock market before the end of 2026, with analysts forecasting a valuation exceeding $2 trillion.

The company’s charter requires its leadership to balance shareholder returns with responsible AI development.

The breakneck speed of AI development has prompted widespread anxiety about possible negative downstream effects on society, including the job market.

In a report published last month, consulting firm McKinsey estimated that up to 11 million American workers may need to switch careers over the next decade due to AI-driven automation.
sources.headline: Anthropic says it will commit 5% of shares to ‘public benefit’ fund

stories.headline: Senegal’s LGBTQ+ people go into hiding amid mass arrests

sources.body:
At least 320 people detained for ‘acts against nature’ after law criminalising homosexuality toughened, HRW reports

Mass arrests, forced HIV testing and barriers to legal representation are part of an escalating crackdown against LGBTQ+ people in Senegal, according to a new report .

More than 320 individuals have been arrested and detained on allegations of “acts against nature” since February, according to HIV Justice Network , an organisation quoted in the Human Rights Watch (HRW) report. Among these, at least 84 were charged with “voluntary HIV transmission”, solely on the basis of their HIV status.

The intensifying crackdown comes as the law criminalising homosexuality in the country was toughened earlier this year. On 11 March, Senegal’s parliament amended the penal code, doubling the maximum prison term for consensual same-sex relations to 10 years.

The new law introduced penalties of up to seven years in prison and a fine of 500,000 to 5m CFA francs (£650–£6,500) for promoting homosexuality, or supporting or financing LGBTQ+ people and organisations.

Larissa Kojoué, LGBTQ+ rights researcher at Human Rights Watch, said: “LGBTQ+ people are being forced to curb their normal activities … for fear of arrest and increased stigma. Senegal’s government should call a halt to this crackdown, which threatens everyone’s rights.”

Same-sex sexual activity was criminalised in Senegal in 1965, but hostility towards LGBTQ+ individuals has grown in recent years. During the 2024 presidential campaign, Bassirou Diomaye Faye, who ended up winning the election, and the former prime minister Ousmane Sonko promised to strengthen laws criminalising same-sex relations , framing the issue as a national priority.

Arrests of men and women have happened all over the country. The police say they have arrested people based on information extracted from seized phones , third-party allegations or raids on private premises.

The changes to the penal code have had a chilling effect on lawyers, who said they were afraid to represent people for fear of being prosecuted themselves, according to the report. Doctors told Human Rights Watch that the changes were discouraging people from seeking HIV testing and treatment.

While there was a 49% fall in new HIV infections in western and central Africa from 2010 to 2022, sub-Saharan Africa remains disproportionately affected by the virus, with 64% of all people living with HIV globally.

Sylvie Beaumont, a consultant with HIV Justice Network, said she had received anecdotal evidence that HIV clinics had seen a drop in attendance. “Obviously this is not good for the HIV response because people are going without treatment, they’re not going to get tested,” she said.

“The consequences are really bad and it’s sad because Senegal was a country that was doing well with their HIV response. They are shooting themselves in the foot.”

She said while the law criminalising deliberate HIV transmission was not part of the reforms to the penal code this year, there had been an “unprecedented” rate of arrests in recent months. She labelled the charges “nonsensical” because it was reported that most people had either only discovered their status upon arrest; were arrested with condoms; or were on treatment that renders transmission of the virus impossible.
sources.headline: LGBTQ+ people go into hiding in Senegal as hundreds are arrested

stories.headline: Democrats test whether Tejano star Bobby Pulido can win back South Texas Latino voters

sources.body: EDINBURG, Texas — A man walks out to a packed arena filled with fervent fans. Nostalgic music blasts out over the speakers as the audience of the spectacle sways and sing along. Firehouse-red campaign hats litter the heads of the devotees jammed in tight to see the show. But this isn’t a MAGA rally, and that’s not Donald Trump hitting the stage. On stage is Bobby Pulido, the Tejano star turned Democratic House candidate clad in head-to-toe leather and a black cowboy hat. The occasion? “La Ultima Desvelada,” what he said will be his final concert in Edinburg on Saturday night. Pulido is trying to flip a district that has steadily, over the past decade, slipped from the grasp of the Democratic Party and became the ultimate swing test for the country’s most culturally conservative Latino voters. If Pulido wins in Texas’ 15th District against incumbent GOP Rep. Monica De La Cruz, the Democratic Party stands to gain much more than just a seat that could make a House majority. As the party looks to rebuild with Latinos and lay the groundwork for 2028, the Tejano crooner could become a strong messenger to one of Democrats’ weakest voting blocs. “Mexican-American men haven't really felt like they have a home,” in either party, Pulido told POLITICO in an interview. “It almost feels like the Latino man wants to be that provider, and he can’t fulfill that right now.” Like many Democrats this cycle, Pulido has dialed in on affordability and an aggressive economic messaging slamming Trump’s tariffs, the war with Iran and the growing stream of big corporate money in political campaigns. But unlike his fellow Democrats, Pulido echoes a social conservatism that has defined the region. He’s “ chapado a la antigua,” he told reporters Friday — a Spanish saying for old-school or traditional. “Those traditions of how [Latino men] were raised are going away, and I think there’s a lot of frustration,” Pulido told POLITICO. “They want somebody to talk to them in the language of, ‘Let me go out there and work, right? So I can provide for my family.’” Pulido has tapped into a level of political fervor and cultural star power for which the Democratic Party has been starved. Trump won the district by a staggering 18 points in 2024 — and it was redrawn by Republicans last year. But Pulido’s near-universal name ID as an Edinburg native and music star, combined with historic headwinds buffeting, put the south Texas district on the map as one of the biggest toss-ups this cycle. With just over two weeks to go, Pulido is in a dead heat against De La Cruz. He’s leaving behind three decades as a musician, multiple Latin Grammys and packed arenas for a shot at representing his hometown in the halls of Congress. The 956 region knows Pulido and his family to an extent that very few would-be members of Congress could boast. They know his father, Roberto Pulido, also a famous Tejano singer who joined his son onstage. They know his uncle, a former county judge. But beyond that, with billions of streams to his name, Pulido’s 90s hits became a ubiquitous sound for the RGV. And only in the RGV would his supporters trot up to the arena on horseback, coming off the nearby expressway. That fame, and his deep district ties, made Pulido one of the party’s most prized recruits this cycle. He’s one of the DCCC’s top candidates, with a campaign staffed in part by blue dog organizations like The Bench while also boasting the same Latino consultants as Sen. Ruben Gallego’s (D-Ariz.) 2024 Senate campaign. And Democrats see the potential for the kind of surrogate Pulido could become on the 2028 campaign trail. Many of the party’s biggest Latino voices — and attention grabbers — are further on the left. “What we haven't had is someone like Bobby Pulido, who's going to come from the moderate wing of the party, that is going to be a rock star,” Gallego told POLITICO. Should Pulido head to D.C. next year, he’d be joining alongside a crop of fresh progressive Democrats who have ridden the wave of democratic socialism in blue enclaves — most notably New York’s Darializa Avila Chevalier and Claire Valdez. “We're not going to agree on everything,” Pulido conceded. But with Texas primed to get even more electoral votes in future presidential cycles, the party’s direction has to “resonate inside the middle of the heartland,” he said. But it’s not only electoral numbers: the early Democratic nominating calendar is heavily Latino, with both New Mexico and Nevada in the lineup. Mexican-American men could help tip the scales in either state. Pulido knows if he pulls off the win, potential 2028 hopefuls will come flocking, asking him how to win over the Rio Grande Valley. Could he see himself backing 2028 presidential candidates if he wins? They’ll have to convince Pulido first. “I will hold any type of endorsement or anything very close to my chest, and I will definitely make sure that I get behind somebody that has a policy that resonates with Hispanics,” Pulido said. Since Pulido released his hit single “Desvelado” in the mid-90s to today, his hometown of Edinburg and its sister cities across the area transformed from a once-reliable blue working class district to a part of the country deeply wary of the Democratic establishment. Latino voters have embraced the economic populism of Trump and other GOP candidates who touted their more conservative values. In 2022, De La Cruz clinched the district for Republicans. By 2024, Democrats lacked an economic message or answers for what many in the area decried as wide-open borders, Pulido told reporters on the sidelines of his rally in Mercedes on Friday. That’s made the stakes for his races all the bigger, with the RGV becoming the ultimate bellwether. “Bobby's politics are different from the way that we have branded ourselves nationally as a party, but I think that's a good thing,” said Melissa Morales of Somos PAC, which has poured millions into Pulido’s race. But Pulido’s campaign has been marred by scandal. He’s taken heat for crude social media posts about women and gay people. Frankie Caballero, one of his former bandmates, was convicted as a child sex offender . Pulido insisted he was not aware of Caballero’s history while he was in the band as a contractor, having not done a background check. Caballero was convicted in 2014, but later returned to performing with Pulido. De La Cruz’s campaign has made Pulido’s ties to Caballero a staple of attacks. “Bobby Pulido had his uncle drop a child rape charge against a friend so he could play in his band. Then he bailed this pedophile out of jail, brought him to a middle school, and looked the other way while he molested children in South Texas. Latinas are choosing Monica De La Cruz, a working mom fighting for their families, over a corrupt scumbag celebrity who will make life more expensive and already put a predator back on the streets because he likes his accordion,” James Shook, De La Cruz’s campaign manager, said in a statement. Pulido was defensive over his past, but apologized for his social media posts in an interview with POLITICO . He has given varied responses on what he knew about why Caballero went to prison. “I apologize for everything that I’ve ever joked about that offended anybody,” Pulido told POLITICO in August. “But I can’t continue to revisit every single one.” With hundreds flocking to Bert Ogden Arena to witness his final show, Pulido’s popularity has hardly dimmed because of it. Multiple voters in attendance who spoke with POLITICO said they had heard the allegations about Pulido and his accordionist, but none said that it was affecting their vote. “It’s unfortunate, but I’m not gonna hold it against Bobby,” said Joe Barrera, a musician from the Pharr-San Juan-Alamo area. Barrera, an independent, added that he’s still undecided between voting for Pulido or De La Cruz — but said he feels “it’s time for a change.” The economy and immigration dominated the reasons why voters in the crowd pledged their support for the singer. The cost of living has gotten “ re pe caro” — super expensive — Frank Trevino, a Democrat from Edinburg, told POLITICO. He and fellow Edinburg voter Felix Sandoval said they knew Pulido’s mother and remembered Bobby as a kid. “We need to support him, God help him,” Sandoval said. Pulido’s final show Saturday was the talk of Edinburg, from the hallways of the nearby inns to the post-concert stop at Whataburger. Clocking in at nearly two hours, it served as a greatest hits replay for the last 30 years of his life — and a trip down memory lane for many of the voters who grew up with him. “Of course I’m emotional, but I’m leaving with no regrets,” Pulido said from the stage. Pulido is simultaneously up for yet another Latin Grammy recognition this year. And for his status as a longtime entertainer, Pulido is not a fan of the comparisons to Trump, who in his words, is “full of shit.” Yet it’s also something his campaign has been (perhaps ironically) leaning into, with “Make Quinceñeras Great Again” hats nodding to what’s become his signature campaign move. With early voting kicking off on Monday, Pulido sharpened his closing pitch: He’s not for Democrats or Republicans — he’s for his district. “I want to give something back to the place that’s given me so much,” Pulido said. “And if you give me the honor of representing you in Congress, I give you my word that I’ll never forget where I came from.”

stories.headline: Raphael Warnock makes a high-risk push for Democrats in Mississippi’s Senate race

sources.body: JACKSON, Mississippi — Raphael Warnock is racing to get Democrat Scott Colom elected in deep-red Mississippi. It’s part of his bigger bet on the South. Colom, a charismatic local prosecutor, is within striking distance in the polls of unseating Republican Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith. And in the absence of more dedicated resources, Warnock himself is trying to fill the gap by directing money and donors to the race. He has raised over $500,000 directly into Colom’s campaign committee, according to a person with direct knowledge of his efforts, granted anonymity to share private details. And, over the course of four separate fundraisers, has tried to steer Senate Democrats’ top donors to the race. In April, he told attendees at a Democratic donor breakfast that he thinks the party is “sleeping on” the Mississippi contest, prompting surprised laughter from the crowd, according to a recording of the event obtained by POLITICO. “I'm going to ask you to resist the Democratic tendency to ignore the South,” he told the assembled donors. “And for our own sake, for the sake of us having a possibility of winning over time, I think we can win in Mississippi if the conditions are just right.” Warnock, who is also widely seen as a potential presidential contender, is trying to capitalize on an incredibly unfavorable midterm environment for the GOP that has put more and more traditionally red states into play. He has been criss-crossing not just Mississippi, but the broader South, to convince Democrats to expand into the region and shore up their support with Black voters ahead of 2028. The time is ripe, he said, for a “new kind of Southern strategy” — a play off of former President Richard Nixon’s plan for Republicans to best Democrats in the region in the late 1960s that capitalized on white backlash to the civil rights movement. It’s been a hard sell so far, particularly in Mississippi: Republicans control all levers of state government, and Trump handily won by 24 points in 2024. The last time Mississippians sent a Democrat to the Senate was 1982. Even though national Democrats speak highly of Colom’s candidacy, their resources to compete on an expanded Senate battleground map are already strained, and money has been prioritized in more expensive, high-profile contests like Iowa, Alaska and Maine. The half-million Warnock has raised for Colom is 15% of the $3.5 million he’s managed to raise over the cycle. It’s still a strategic move on Warnock’s part: An upset win by Colom would boost the Senator’s own profile as he continues to leave the door open to running for president. And even if Colom loses, the South is a treasure trove of delegates for 2028 — and Black voters dominate the region in Democratic primaries. Pressed whether he’s interested in the White House himself, Warnock evaded, saying he’s “trying to think and pray about the highest and best use of my skills.” “I’ve been at crossroads many times, and in the moment, I've always known what to do,” he added. Other Democrats see the work as helpful regardless of what Warnock does in 2028. “The ’28 chatter is something he will listen to, but I don't think it's something that's part of a checklist he's marching towards,” said Georgia Democratic strategist Andrew Heaton, who has worked on Warnock’s Senate campaigns. “Regardless of what happens on that front, ’28 is going to be a very busy year because — especially if he decides not to run — I think there's no question he's planning on running for the Senate again.” Free from the constraints of reelection this year, Warnock has traveled across the Carolinas, Mississippi and his Georgia home to support local candidates and pitch a vision of his party’s future that runs through the region that launched his political career. In interviews with POLITICO on the campaign trail, Warnock drew parallels between Democrats’ 2020 wins in Georgia — his own, Sen. Jon Ossoff’s and former President Joe Biden’s — and the conditions he sees emerging in the Magnolia State for Democratic growth. Those kinds of wins will disappear from the horizon if Democrats fail to invest now and in the Black voters who are core to the party’s coalition, he argued. Mississippi, where over 35% of the population is Black, would be key to the Democratic Party’s efforts to win back voters of color, as many shifted toward Trump and Republicans in 2024. Strong Democratic candidates have reached around 45% of the vote in the state in recent years, but none have been able to punch through for a victory in Mississippi, which has a long history of extremely polarized voting along racial lines. But in the wake of the Supreme Court’s decision to gut the Voting Rights Act, there are signs Black voters are surging to the polls in higher numbers — and some Democrats hope that could remake the state’s politics. “It is in the interest of the party to invest in the base and have the base understand that the party understands that these are loyal Democratic voters, and Black voters want what other voters want,” said Warnock. “They want the same kind of prosperity and opportunity that all families want.” Colom was more blunt. Asked if he equates ignoring Mississippi and its Senate race to the party ignoring Black voters, he said: “Yeah, of course, 100 percent.” Democrats have not been averse to flooding money into traditionally red states in the final stretch of the campaign, but Mississippi has not yet made it high on that list, where Colom still faces an uphill battle to close the gap with Hyde-Smith. Building out the statewide grassroots infrastructure that has proved effective in places like Georgia takes time and resources, which have yet to land in Mississippi at a significant scale this cycle. “Democrats are investing in Mississippi, but not enough. And, I think, certainly not as much as I think we should, and not as much as we could,” Warnock said in an interview between campaign stops in the state. He was in somewhat of a rush: between a fundraiser for Colom and an event with local faith leaders, Warnock wanted to visit the home of Medgar Evers, the civil rights era titan who was shot and killed in the car port of his Jackson home in 1963. “We're playing enough here to force the other side to compete in Mississippi, and that is an improvement, but it's not enough,” he said. Colom himself has begged national Democrats to focus on his race. “Mississippi has really always been competitive. It just hasn't got the attention, the resources it deserves,” Colom said in an interview at his campaign headquarters. Some has come: American Bridge, a Democrat-aligned super PAC, pumped over $2 million into the race earlier this month, and earlier this week the New York Times reported that a single megadonor is set to split $7 million of his personal wealth between Colom’s race and others. Several top Democrats have made an effort to signal their support. Former Vice President Kamala Harris and former Secretary of Transportation Pete Buttigieg plan to visit the state before Election Day. Senate Majority Leader Chuck Schumer and his Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee chair, Kirsten Gillibrand, have each hosted separate fundraisers for Colom, according to a source familiar with the events, granted anonymity to share private details. And Delaware Sen. Lisa Blunt Rochester, a DSCC vice-chair, campaigned with Colom in Mississippi. Colom’s campaign committee outraised Hyde-Smith’s over the summer, posting $1.3 million to her just over $640,000 . But it pales in comparison to the tens of millions that have flooded into other states. In separate statements, spokespeople for the DSCC and Senate Majority PAC lauded Colom as a strong candidate, but said they were constrained by how much they could spend. Both groups said they were monitoring the race “closely.” Republicans are still publicly maintaining their confidence in their hold on the seat. Jake Monssen, Hyde-Smith’s campaign manager, tied Colom to Washington Democrats in a statement and said the campaign “planned for Colom to have plenty of resources. We are executing our own campaign plan with that in mind.” One day after his sojourn in Mississippi, Warnock was presented with a stark contrast in what Democrats are capable of when they devote resources to a Southern state. He was in North Carolina on Thursday, where Democratic Senate nominee Roy Cooper is dominating his Republican opponent , Michael Whatley, in fundraising and polling. As one of Democrats’ top candidate recruits of the cycle, Cooper has attracted significant resources and national attention from the outset of the race. But Mississippi and North Carolina are two enormously different states, in population, income, and demographics — and that change didn’t happen overnight. Democrats began significantly investing in the state ever since President Barack Obama’s 2008 victory there and ramped up their efforts after the GOP-led state government redrew the state’s congressional maps in 2013. “It's taken a lot over the last 13 years,” Rep. Valerie Foushee (D-N.C.) said on the sidelines of a party canvass kickoff in Durham. “Our eye has never been taken off the ball, and because we believe that we could make that change, that we needed to be the change that we wanted to see, we have put that in action now, and we're going to win because of it.”
sources.headline: Can Scott Colom win Mississippi Senate? Warnock is making a big bet on it.

stories.headline: Alaska Senator Dan Sullivan embraces Trump while facing a close reelection race

sources.body: GIRDWOOD, Alaska — Dan Sullivan isn’t running away from President Donald Trump like so many other vulnerable Republicans. He’s betting that walking the line instead will help him reap reelection in November. During a candidate debate, speaking at an economic forum and in an interview with Playbook this week, Sullivan repeatedly denied chances to put distance between himself and Trump’s most unpopular policies and positions. Has the economic pain from the war with Iran been worth it for Alaskans? “The real economic pain is when Democrats get control,” Sullivan told POLITICO, sitting in the shadow of a well-antlered taxidermy moose head, next to a roaring fire, at a ski resort tucked up in the mountains off the Turnagain Arm southeast of Anchorage. What about the $5,000 dividends Trump has promised voters if Republicans hold control of Congress, as he did at a rally for Sullivan in Wasilla on Tuesday? “I’ve got to look at the legislation. I don't know,” Sullivan said. “That was the first time I heard it from him, and I would just evaluate that if and when it happens.” Does he want to see data centers — which Trump has pushed for further development despite some pushback from local communities — pop up on Alaska’s undeveloped land? He’s not putting his foot down. “They definitely got to pay their own way in terms of energy,” Sullivan said. “They have to have local input and approval, and we’ll see.” Still, Sullivan bristled on some issues that touch closer to home. In light of Trump’s decision to import Russian diesel, did Sullivan think the Trump administration was being too friendly with Russia? “I thought you were asking me campaign stuff,” Sullivan replied. “Is this like a hit piece or what?” “I know my view on Russia. I'm very hawkish on Russia,” Sullivan continued, pointing to an op-ed he wrote during Trump's first administration about whether the president was too close with Russian President Vladimir Putin. “I wrote an op-ed essentially saying, sometimes I don't agree with the rhetoric, but at the end of the day, what does Putin understand? He understands power. What's the ultimate source of power that the Russians fear? U.S. military power, which Republicans always build up, Democrats always cut.” Though his office put out a statement decrying the diesel move, Sullivan didn’t sign a bipartisan letter calling on the president to reverse the decision — which he said he never saw — and instead took his concerns straight to the White House. “I speak to the administration all the time on the issues of high energy costs,” Sullivan said. Art Hackney, a veteran Republican strategist in Alaska who runs a pro-Sullivan super PAC called “We Stand with Dan,” said in an interview that another part of the calculus is that Murkowski has provided a straightforward example of how Trump treats Republicans who publicly disagree with him. “If Dan did something considered a disrespectful trigger or something, what do you think would happen? It could well have implications for things that affect Alaska's economy.” But Trump, for better or worse, is a centerpiece of races like Sullivan’s. The president has pleaded with voters at rallies to “pretend I'm on the ballot” — just as he did alongside Sullivan on Tuesday. And Alaska’s tighter-than-expected Senate race is poised to be a linchpin for deciding which party holds control of the chamber. Alaska, Ohio and Iowa are the races that Trump officials view as increasingly critical to keep their majority, according to three GOP officials familiar with the Trump-aligned super PAC MAGA Inc.’s strategy, granted anonymity to candidly assess the midterms. Sullivan only sees Trump’s presence as a boon. “I think the rally certainly helps in terms of energizing the base,” Sullivan said. He’s proud to have the president campaign alongside him, plus Vice President JD Vance, HHS Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. and Sen. Ted Cruz (R-Texas). “I'm bringing up my people,” Sullivan said. “I’m not afraid of that.” Polls show Sullivan tied with or trailing former Rep. Mary Peltola, one of Democrats’ top hopes to help flip the Senate. On paper, this contest shouldn’t be close: Peltola lost her House seat after just one term. “It was Trump plus-13 two years ago, so it is not the position we’d love to be in, but we’re doing what we do to help get him across the finish line,” said Kevin Greene, the state director for Americans for Prosperity-Alaska, which has knocked on tens of thousands of doors for Sullivan. On one such door-to-door trip with Greene in Anchorage on Thursday morning, voters across approximately a dozen houses were about evenly split between supporting Sullivan or Peltola. Only one agreed to speak on the record to POLITICO: John Baker, a 67-year-old retiree who said he used to be a Republican but would be supporting Peltola this year. What happened? “Donald Trump happened,” Baker said. He added that his support for Peltola was 70% because he wanted to see Democrats take the Senate and 30% because he liked her as a candidate. Peltola, the first Alaska Native to represent the state in Congress, has centered her campaign around “fish, family, and freedom” while capitalizing on voters’ frustrations with the high cost of energy and goods, particularly in remote communities. She has focused on outreach to villages in the Alaskan bush and has largely shied away from national attention, including from the media. The former congresswoman has some major liabilities that Sullivan often slams. Just two years ago, she lost her reelection bid after only one full term. She has sought to distance herself from the Biden administration, which remains unpopular in the state. She has a reputation for missing meetings and votes. And a New York Times report last month alleged that she created a hostile work environment and regularly used slurs and other offensive language. Even those close to her campaign, though optimistic, acknowledge it’s still an uphill battle. “It’s always been long odds,” said John-Henry Heckendorn, a Democratic strategist in Alaska whose firm is supporting Peltola outside of her official campaign. Peltola, he said, would have to do about twice as well as the Democratic Senate challengers in the past four cycles in order to win. At the debate on Thursday, Peltola said she “prided” herself on being “available to Alaskan press” — though she acknowledged she has “really demurred from national attention, from national outlets.” After the debate, POLITICO asked Peltola: “You said you’re accessible to the press. Will you take some questions?” She smiled, then walked away quickly, with an aide saying she had a dinner to attend. “She’s hoping that the Joe Biden bunker mentality will win, and you know, maybe it will,” Sullivan told POLITICO on Friday. “I don't think it will. I think Alaskans can see through it.” Peltola’s campaign declined several interview requests for this story. In an email to POLITICO, the campaign noted that Sullivan was in the top quarter of most-absent senators , and that Peltola had to miss congressional votes when both her husband and mother died. The email also noted that Peltola helped secure the Willow oil-drilling project and has a record of bucking her fellow Democrats. Peltola has hosted at least 16 events in Alaska this month, the campaign said, and has interviewed with eight news outlets in the past week. “Dan Sullivan has tripled his wealth in the Senate and voted fourteen times for the war in Iran that is raising costs one everything from gas to groceries, Mary has been talking with Alaskans in every corner of the state about her plan to take on the rigged system in DC, lower costs, and put Alaska first,” Harry Child, a campaign spokesperson, said in a statement to POLITICO. Sullivan is leaning on his strong legislative record and support for oil and gas development in the state. He has sought to tie Peltola to Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer, Joe Biden and Kamala Harris, and has attributed her massive fundraising edge to “lower-48 liberal millionaires and billionaires who want to turn Alaska into national parks.” Though he’s largely embracing Trump, there’s still moments of disagreement. But even in those spaces, he’s touting his close ties to the White House and effectiveness as a Washington operator instead of pushing the president away. Sullivan was opposed to Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth’s plan to livestream the execution of the convicted Fort Hood shooter, and told POLITICO “there’s probably no senator weighing in more with senior White House and directly with the Secretary of War than me, saying this is not a good idea.” Trump called off the livestream on Thursday . Trump’s approval rating here, like the country at large, is underwater. The war with Iran has hit Alaska hard, where nearly all goods are imported by plane or barge, with urban gas prices hovering around $5 per gallon and prices in the bush often double that. In a year when Republican voters may be more likely to stay home without Trump on the ballot — Democrats eye an opening. “We have a golden opportunity with a fantastic candidate on our end and a really mediocre one on theirs,” said Alaska Democratic Party Chair Eric Croft. “I think we've been coming that way for a long time, and this is our chance to pump through.” Trump on Tuesday flew more than eight hours from Washington to Wasilla, home of Sarah Palin and the Iditarod, with Interior Secretary Doug Burgum, Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick, FCC Chair Brendan Carr and FHFA Administrator Bill Pulte in tow. He announced that Taiwan had joined South Korea in its commitments to a proposed Alaska energy pipeline — though the project is still in flux — and that the FCC will vote this month to invest an additional $162 million to expand high-speed internet in the state. Thousands of the president’s fans piled into the ice hockey rink and thousands more gathered outside, watching Trump speak on a jumbotron. Asked by POLITICO what he thought about Peltola, rally attendee Jeff Caswell, 59, replied: “I don’t.” But in a state where independents outnumber Republicans, that enthusiasm may only go so far. “Very conservative MAGA voters can’t vote for you harder,” said Scott Kendall, a veteran political strategist who worked on two of Alaska GOP Sen. Lisa Murkowski’s campaigns and was chief of staff to former Alaska Gov. Bill Walker. “Donald Trump’s support in this current climate is both a blessing and a curse,” Kendall noted. Even some reliable Trump supporters at the rally acknowledged the outlook appeared bleak. “I think Alaska’s turning blue,” Matt Niessink, a 45-year-old general contractor from Wasilla, said at the rally. He said he had voted for Trump three times and planned to support Republicans this year. What did he wish the president would do differently? “I wish he’d shut his mouth sometimes and not be such a pompous ass,” Niessink said.

stories.headline: Spain’s Constitutional Court considers intervening over voting rights for 160,000 citizens under the ‘grandchildren law’

sources.body:
“El vínculo entre ser español y el voto es indisoluble”, defiende el Defensor del Pueblo en su demanda de amparo ante el tribunal de garantías, que decide desde hoy si admite ese recurso o si deben agotarse primero otras vías

“El vínculo entre ser español y el voto es indisoluble”, afirma el Defensor del Pueblo en su recurso de amparo ante el Tribunal Constitucional en defensa del derecho al voto de más de 160.000 españoles que residen en el extranjero y a quienes el Tribunal Supremo ha privado cautelarmente del sufragio. Todos son españoles y el Defensor considera que lo son “pacíficamente incluso para las partes” que recurrieron ante el Supremo —los partidos Vox y Iustitia Europa— quienes “cuestionan solo” una Instrucción del Ministerio de Justicia con indicaciones para la aplicación de la llamada ley de nietos de 2022. Para el Defensor, es “harto problemática” la suspensión del sufragio a los descendientes de exiliados de la posguerra nacionalizados en virtud de dicha ley. Muchos ya votaron en 2023 .

“La condición de votante no la puede perder ningún español mientras lo sea, pues ni siquiera el Código Penal prevé la pena de pérdida del sufragio activo (elegir), sino del pasivo (ser elegido)”, explica el recurso del Defensor presentado el viernes y que pide, dada la “urgencia excepcional” del asunto, que el Constitucional lo admita sin escuchar a las partes afectadas, según prevé su Ley Orgánica (art. 56.6).

Casi todo en este asunto carece de precedentes. La retirada de un plumazo del derecho de voto a más de 160.000 nacionales por una Instrucción que llevaba cuatro años en vigor; la vía utilizada: un recurso contencioso-adminstrativo contra una resolución de la Junta Electoral Central de julio pasado que ha acabado afectando a las prerrogativas de la nacionalidad ; el momento, a poco más de un mes de las elecciones generales del 29 de noviembre , y las consecuencias excepcionales que podrían desatarse: un conflicto entre el Supremo y el Constitucional que necesariamente se proyectaría sobre la definición del censo, y que podría abrir múltiples vías de impugnación incluso tras los comicios del 29-N.

Lo primero, habrá que resolver si el recurso de amparo del Defensor es prematuro o no. Presentado el viernes , la admisión del recurso se discutirá a partir de este lunes, cuando se espera que el ponente comparta su postura inicial con sus dos compañeros de la Sección Cuarta. Si no hubiera unanimidad entre los tres magistrados —el ponente, Enrique Arnaldo, del bloque conservador; y los dos del progresista, María Luisa Balaguer y Ramón Sáez—, la decisión sobre la admisibilidad se elevaría a la Sala, también con mayoría progresista.

Fuentes del Constitucional consideran que todas las posibilidades están abiertas, aunque es previsible que se avoque al Pleno y se resuelva el miércoles. El recurso plantea dudas procesales porque no está claro que se hayan agotado todas las vías ordinarias, y ello es requisito para su admisión.

El Defensor del Pueblo considera que sí se han agotado, porque los autos del Supremo —el del 12 de octubre, y el del 10 de septiembre pasados— son firmes y no cabe recurso contra ellos. El Supremo, sin embargo, abrió un trámite de alegaciones para los afectados el 12 de octubre. Ese ofrecimiento, subraya el Defensor, no sería más que un modo de parchear lo que ya debería haberse hecho en septiembre. En el primer auto no se daba audiencia a los afectados, aunque entonces no había elecciones a la vista y la materialización de la suspensión no era inminente.
sources.headline: El Constitucional discute si intervenir ya en la controversia sobre la suspensión del derecho al voto de 160.000 españoles por la ‘ley de nietos’

sources.body:
Vox ha presentado un escrito ante el Tribunal Constitucional para que inadmita el recurso de amparo interpuesto por el Defensor del Pueblo contra las resoluciones del Supremo que suspendieron el derecho a voto de los nacionalizados mediante la denominada ley de nietos .

En un comunicado difundido este domingo, el partido que lidera Santiago Abascal sostiene que el recurso es "prematuro", ya que el Tribunal Supremo mantiene abierto hasta el 22 de octubre el plazo para que los afectados puedan personarse y formular alegaciones.

Asimismo, considera que no se ha acreditado una lesión constitucional actual ni se ha justificado suficientemente la especial trascendencia constitucional del recurso.

Vox defiende que las medidas acordadas por el Supremo buscan "preservar la legalidad, objetividad y transparencia del censo electoral, sin anular la nacionalidad española ni establecer una exclusión definitiva de los electores afectados".

En este sentido, recuerda que el Alto Tribunal apreció un "peligro fundado, real y serio de poder afectar gravemente a la objetividad y transparencia del proceso electoral".

Por ello, esta formación solicita la inadmisión del recurso o, subsidiariamente, su desestimación, así como el rechazo de las medidas cautelarísimas y cautelares solicitadas por el Defensor del Pueblo, al considerar que podrían comprometer la correcta conformación del censo de cara a las elecciones del 29 de noviembre.

El líder de Vox, Santiago Abascal, se ha congratulado en una entrevista en La Razón de haber conseguido "derrotar la ley de nietos" y advierte de que "Sánchez tienen más conejos en la chistera para alterar el resultado de las elecciones".

Así, ha insistido en que las elecciones del 29 de noviembre "no van a ser unos comicios limpios" porque Sánchez "tiene la intención de seguir haciendo trampas y mintiendo sin límite para ganar".

" Serán unas elecciones con violencia , con mucha presión en las calles. El Gobierno usará a sus milicias porque quieren que haya violencia entorno a Vox, atemorizar a nuestra gente y relacionarnos con la bronca", afirma.
sources.headline: Vox pide al Constitucional que inadmita el recurso del Defensor del Pueblo sobre la ley de nietos

stories.headline: Government prepares decree to improve survivor, disability and violence-victim benefits

sources.body:
El Ejecutivo usará todos los Consejos de Ministros hasta las elecciones del 29-N para aprobar hitos como la subida del Salario Mínimo Interprofesional

El Gobierno se ha tomado muy en serio la idea que lanzó Pedro Sánchez el mismo día que convocó las elecciones . Esto es, que piensa “seguir gobernando hasta las elecciones”. El martes pasado, el Consejo de Ministros no tuvo mucho contenido político ni decisiones de calado porque era un día especial en el que toda l a actualidad estaba centrada en la visita de los Reyes a Ceuta. Pero a partir de esta semana, el Gobierno, según diversas fuentes, empieza una secuencia que ya no parará hasta las elecciones de lo que se ha llamado internamente como “martes sociales”. Esto se traduce en que en cada Consejo de Ministros se aprobarán medidas que han propuesto los ministerios y que habían quedado pendientes para poder sacarlas adelante antes de los comicios del 29-N.

El Ejecutivo cuenta con la ventaja de que los decretos ley que apruebe, como ya hizo hace dos semanas con los de vivienda, pueden ser convalidados por una diputación permanente más favorable que el pleno de Congreso, porque ahí los votos de Junts son irrelevantes. Basta con convencer a la izquierda y al PNV.

Este martes, según fuentes del Gobierno, ya irá un paquete importante de medidas del Ministerio de Seguridad Social en forma de decreto ley, y por tanto con necesidad de ser convalidado antes de un mes por la diputación permanente.

Todas ellas son ampliaciones de derechos o mejoras de condiciones de pensiones para distintos colectivos importantes. Con este decreto, por ejemplo, se ampliará la incapacidad temporal para mujeres que sufren patologías asociadas a la menopausia; y para víctimas de violencia de género, que tendrán una prestación del 60% de la base reguladora hasta el día 20 de la baja y del 75% a partir de entonces. La empresa abonará el salario el día de la baja, pero a partir de entonces, la Seguridad Social abonará la prestación, señala el Gobierno.

Se mejorará, además, la prestación para padres y madres por cuidado de menores con cáncer o enfermedades graves. Los dos progenitores podrán recibirla de forma alternativa o simultánea. En casos de mayor vulnerabilidad, podrá mantenerse más allá de los 26 años cuando la persona afectada presente una dependencia de grado III o una discapacidad especialmente elevada.

Se ampliará el acceso a las pensiones de viudedad en caso de parejas de hecho. A partir de ahora, la existencia de hijos en común será suficiente para acreditar la realidad de una pareja de hecho para acceder a esta prestación, algo que en la actualidad estaba generando problemas. Las solicitudes que fueron denegadas podrán ser revisadas en los próximos 12 meses.

Se mejoran también las pensiones extraordinarias derivadas de actos terroristas. A partir de ahora, ninguna de estas pensiones podrá situarse por debajo del equivalente a dos salarios mínimos (2.442 euros), una cantidad un 36% mayor al que había ahora, que quedó desfasado.
sources.headline: El Gobierno arranca los “martes sociales” con un decreto para mejorar las prestaciones por viudedad, incapacidad, para víctimas del terrorismo y de violencia de género

stories.headline: Ceuta hospital sends judge injury reports from migrants alleging military assaults

sources.body:
Los informes médicos, que identifican a las víctimas y detallan sus heridas, son claves para la investigación judicial

La investigación sobre las presuntas agresiones sufridas por inmigrantes en Ceuta a manos de militares puede dar un vuelco con la documentación que el único hospital público de la ciudad autónoma ha remido al juzgado de guardia. Según ha podido saber EL PAÍS, el centro hospitalario ha puesto en conocimiento de la Justicia al menos una veintena de partes médicos en los que figuran las identidades de las víctimas, las lesiones que presentaban y su declaración de que las heridas fueron causadas por miembros del Ejército que realizaban patrullas de vigilancia en Ceuta . Hasta ahora, las denuncias difundidas tenía carácter anónimo y carecían de informes médicos que las avalaran, lo que abocaba la investigación a un callejón sin salida.

Desde que el 30 y 31 de julio pasados se produjo una entrada masiva de más de 70.000 personas en la ciudad autónoma, han circulado por redes sociales y medios de comunicación vídeos en los que se ve a uniformados golpeando a inmigrantes; audios en los que supuestos soldados se jactan de haberles pegado y discuten si es mejor hacerlo con la mano desnuda o con guantes; e imágenes de adultos y menores de edad que muestran las heridas y moratones que han dejado en su cuerpo los golpes que dicen haber recibido por parte de militares. La ONG defensora de los derechos humanos Amnistía Internacional (AI) difundió el pasado 30 de septiembre un informe con evidencias de malos tratos e incluso torturas a inmigrantes y refugiados por parte de miembros de las Fuerzas Armadas basado en 22 testimonios recogidos por sus investigadores sobre el terreno. El Ministerio de Defensa ha remitido tanto el informe de AI como los audios difundidos por eldiario.es al juzgado de guardia ceutí y a la Fiscalía.

No obstante, todo este material acusatorio, que apuntaría a una práctica extendida entre militares cuya misión en Ceuta es de vigilancia, disuasión y apoyo a las Fuerzas de Seguridad del Estado ante la anómala situación que vive la ciudad desde hace casi doce semanas, adolece de una grave carencia: no se identifica a los agresores, ni siquiera a la unidad militar a la que pertenecen. Y lo que es más importante aún: no se revela la identidad de las víctimas, lo que hace muy difícil verificarla.

Los inmigrantes tienen miedo a represalias y cuando relatan su experiencia ante ONG o periodistas ponen como condición ocultar su rostro la mayoría de las veces y su nombre siempre. Tampoco acuden a la Policía para denunciar la paliza que dicen haber recibido por temor a ser expulsados del territorio español, al que entraron irregularmente.

Sin poder localizar a las víctimas para que ratifiquen en el juzgado la denuncia que hicieron ante la prensa o las ONG y sin poder someterlas a un examen médico para verificar las lesiones sufridas como consecuencia de las supuestas agresiones, las diligencias en curso estaban abocadas al fracaso, reconocen fuentes jurídicas. Sin embargo, la investigación puede desbloquearse gracias a la documentación del Hospital Universitario de Ceuta, el único centro hospitalario público de la ciudad, que gestiona el Ingesa (Instituto Nacional de Gestión Sanitaria), dependiente del Ministerio de Sanidad, ya que la sanidad no está transferida a las autoridades locales.
sources.headline: El hospital de Ceuta remite al juez una veintena de partes de lesiones de inmigrantes que dicen haber sido agredidos por militares

stories.headline: Government accelerates national electricity-grid expansion before the election

sources.body:
La vicepresidenta y ministra para la Transición Ecológica, Sara Aagesen. / José Luis Roca

El Gobierno trabaja para aprobar ‘in extremis’ la gran ampliación de las redes eléctricas antes de las elecciones del próximo 29 de noviembre, pese a las dudas legales que había por cómo presentar el proyecto definitivo al Congreso de los Diputados tras la disolución de las Cortes por el adelanto de los comicios . El Ministerio para la Transición Ecológica, comandado por la vicepresidenta Sara Aagesen, zanja ahora el debate legal y confirma su objetivo de sacar adelante la nueva planificación eléctrica hasta 2030 antes del 29-N.

El Gobierno ya ha presentado la propuesta definitiva del ‘ megaplán’ de ampliación y modernización de la red de transporte de electricidad, la que gestiona Red Eléctrica de España. Un programa que ahora contempla una inversión histórica de más de 17.000 millones de euros (3.400 millones más que la primera versión del plan , y más del doble que la planificación vigente con 8.200 millones) y con 6.700 kilómetros de nuevo mallado,. El objetivo es extender una infraestructura clave para seguir conectando nuevas plantas renovables y para poder enchufar los proyectos industriales, tecnológicos y promociones de vivienda que se acumulan, por los problemas de saturación de la actual red.

La aprobación definitiva del plan, tras el largo proceso de tramitación y tras atender un aluvión de más de 2.500 alegaciones, se articula a través de un simple acuerdo de Consejo de Ministros , que -como ha insistido el presidente Pedro Sánchez y otros miembros del Ejecutivo- va a seguir gobernando a pesar del adelanto electoral. Pero antes del ‘ok’ final del Consejo de Ministros, el texto a de ser presentado al Congreso de los Diputados para su examen y debate. Y esto es lo que había generado dudas legales acerca de si la aprobación podía seguir adelante en este momento de impasse en las Cámaras.

La regulación contempla que la vicepresidenta Sara Aagesen presente al Congreso de los Diputados el proyecto para su debate, aunque no pueda vetarlo. En principio, la presentación a la Cámara Baja de la planificación se realiza en la comisión para la Transición Ecológica . Pero disueltas las Cortes esa comisión no funciona, y no estaba claro que pudiera ser presentada a la Diputación Permanente del Congreso, que es el órgano que sigue actuando en periodo preelectoral y hasta la constitución de las nuevas Cámaras. En la normativa simplemente no está prevista esta casuística.

Tras un análisis jurídico, el Gobierno ha zanjado el debate y considera que la Diputación Permanente del Consejo sí que tiene potestad para atender la presentación de la nueva planificación eléctrica y la intención gubernamental es hacerlo en las próximas semanas para acelerar la aprobación definitiva de la planificación, según confirman fuentes oficiales a EL PERIÓDICO.

El Ministerio para la Transición Ecológica había iniciado la presentación de la versión definitiva del plan a los gobiernos de todas las comunidades autónomas ya antes de la convocatoria adelantada de las elecciones. El departamento de Aagesen paralizó los encuentros con las administraciones regionales durante unos días a la espera de saber si podría seguir adelante con la aprobación por la disolución de las Cámaras, pero ahora los ha reactivado con un auténtico acelerón en la agenda. En los últimos días, la ronda de presentaciones a las CCAA se ha reimpulsado, incluso celebrando varios encuentros en un mismo día. La presentación de las actuaciones territorializadas de la planificación no es un trámite obligatorio, pero sí se considera una cortesía que el Ministerio ha decidido mantener pese a pretender acelerar el proceso para la aprobación.
sources.headline: El Gobierno acelera para lanzar ‘in extremis’ la gran ampliación de las redes eléctricas antes de las elecciones

sources.headline: Troben 30 quilos de coure en un gestor de residus i Adif sospita que podrien ser robats

sources.body:
Els Mossos d'Esquadra han detingut dues persones, de 41 i 17 anys, acusades de robar 134 quilos de coure de les vies del tren a prop de la nova estació de la Sagrera, al districte de Sant Andreu de Barcelona.

El 5 d'octubre, un testimoni va alertar agents de la comissaria de Sant Andreu que havia vist dues persones encaputxades que saltaven una tanca i accedien a la zona de vies per robar coure. El material que havien sostret l'emmagatzemaven en bosses amagades per la zona.

Els agents es van adreçar a una deixalleria de la zona on sospitaven que els lladres poguessin anar per vendre el coure. Quan van arribar a la deixalleria, vestits de paisà, van veure dues persones que coincidien amb la descripció que havia facilitat el testimoni.

D'aquesta manera van poder enxampar els lladres in fraganti . Acabaven de lliurar el material, valorat en 1.246 euros, i esperaven per cobrar els diners. El coure va quedar intervingut.

Un dels detinguts, el menor de 17 anys, tenia una ordre vigent de recerca i detenció per un robatori amb força, mentre que l'altre acumula antecedents per fets similars i ha passat a disposició judicial el 8 d'octubre.

L'actuació policial, a càrrec de la Unitat d'Investigació de l'Àrea Regional de Transport Urbà i de la comissaria de Sant Andreu, s'emmarca en el Pla Via. Entre els mesos de gener i agost s'han detingut 58 persones i s'han fet 229 denúncies per robatori de coure a la xarxa ferroviària catalana.

L'1 d'agost es va posar en marxa el Pla Via, un pla estratègic i integral, amb la participació dels Mossos d'Esquadra, Adif, policies locals, estament judicial i el gremi d'empreses dedicades a la gestió de residus, per actuar contra aquesta mena de robatoris. Els lladres de coure provoquen afectacions al trànsit de trens i causen un gran perjudici a la mobilitat de la població.

El Pla Via té tres principals línies d'atac per prevenir els robatoris o identificar-ne els culpables en cas que s'hagin produït. I també preveu vigilar els punts de compravenda del coure.
sources.headline: Enxampen in fraganti dos lladres de coure quan intentaven vendre'l a una deixalleria a la Sagrera

stories.headline: Adif expects full restoration of Barcelona–Madrid high-speed rail after train fire

sources.body:
Una setmana després de l'incendi en un tren d'alta velocitat entre Madrid i Barcelona que va afectar milers de passatgers, Adif preveu aquest dilluns restablir la circulació ferroviària per les dues vies entre les localitats de Ricla i Plasencia de Jalón, a l'Aragó.

Aquest tram es va veure afectat per l'incendi a la part final d'un tren de Renfe a les 16.05 hores del passat dilluns, en plena operació tornada del pont del 12 d'octubre, i va obligar a suspendre la circulació per les dues vies durant gairebé cinc hores.

El servei es va recuperar posteriorment, per una única via, però milers de passatgers van viure una odissea d'hores per poder tornar a casa . Els retards i cancel·lacions en el servei entre Barcelona i Madrid han durat tota la setmana.

Segons ha informat Adif aquest diumenge, després de l'incendi, Renfe va avaluar la situació per iniciar els treballs de retirada de la part útil del tren i des de la nit del 15 d'octubre, de la part incendiada.

Segons Adif, tant la retirada del material com les operacions de restitució de la infraestructura danyada han estat de gran complexitat , ja que s'han fet principalment de nit.

La previsió és restablir la circulació per via doble al llarg de la jornada d'aquest dilluns i posar-la a disposició de les operadores ferroviàries com Ouigo i Iryo, amb la finalitat que puguin oferir els seus serveis comercials.

Això permetria recupera r l'oferta comercial, freqüències i temps de l'alta velocitat.
sources.headline: Adif preveu recuperar del tot demà l'alta velocitat Barcelona-Madrid, una setmana després de l'incendi d'un tren

stories.headline: Barcelona’s 246 newcomer classrooms support recently arrived students’ language learning and integration

sources.body: Les escoles i instituts ja fa anys que són testimonis de les onades migratòries viscudes els últims anys. Cada vegada més alumnes d’arreu del món arriben als centres i necessiten una atenció més personalitzada: per aprendre la llengua, però també per integrar-se en un entorn completament nou. A Barcelona hi ha 246 aules d’acollida . Una d’aquestes es troba a l’institut Icària, que ja fa més de 10 anys que té aquest espai per garantir l’aprenentatge intensiu del català, dels coneixements bàsics i la incorporació progressiva de l’alumnat a l’aula ordinària. “L’aula d’acollida ens ajuda a integrar aquest alumnat perquè segueixi els estudis d’una manera eficaç i que pugui sortir de l’institut amb un nivell acceptable”, explica Àlvar Martín, director de l’institut . També et pot interessar El nou curs escolar 2026-27, a punt: més professors, rècord d’aules d’acollida i límits a la IA Redacció 3 minuts de lectura “Ens han ajudat molt” Per als alumnes aquest recurs es converteix en un espai de referència que els permet sentir-se més a gust i amb confiança a l’institut. “He començat a parlar català molt bé, escriure i llegir. Ara sé moltes coses que altres alumnes o companys no saben”, explica l ‘Umme , de Pakistán, que va arribar a l’institut fa tres anys. A la Suri, de Colòmbia, també li agrada molt poder dedicar unes hores a l’aula d’acollida que assegura que li ha faciltat poder conversar amb els companys. “La Pilar (la tutora) és com si fos una mare per mi perquè sempre està per nosaltres i ens ha ajudat molt”, afegeix. Cada aula d’acollida té assignada un tutor o tutora que és qui s’encarrega de planificar el curs, tenint en compte les necessitats de cada un dels alumnes i aplicant les metodologies d’immersió lingüística , i estratègies d’inclusió social . La Pilar Poy , tutora de l’aula d’acollida de l’institut Icària, explica que es posa el focus en els aspectes emocionals: “És molt important aquesta vessant més social i emocional perquè això també ajuda que ells vulguin aprendre una llengua nova i s’integrin amb més facilitat dins de l’entorn dels seus iguals”.
